Contrastive self-supervised methods like SimCLR and MoCo learn representations by pulling together augmented views of the same image while pushing apart views of different images — but this objective implicitly weights samples by how often they appear as negatives, which in a class-imbalanced dataset means rare-class examples are consistently outvoted by the majority. The central question is whether the learned feature space systematically suppresses discriminative features of minority classes — not by ignoring them entirely, but by encoding them at lower magnitude or in directions that are crowded out by majority-class variance. Key concepts include the alignment-uniformity decomposition of contrastive loss, the role of the negative sampling distribution in shaping the hypersphere geometry, and the distinction between representation of a class (does it have a separable cluster?) versus feature richness (does the encoder preserve the fine-grained within-class variation that downstream tasks need?). A beginner worries about whether the minority class appears in the training data; an expert worries about something subtler — that the minority class does appear, produces a cluster that looks clean in UMAP, yet the encoder has discarded the precise features that would allow a fine-grained downstream task to work, because those features never had to be preserved to minimize the contrastive objective across a majority-dominated negative pool. The further danger is that standard linear-probe evaluation on balanced test sets masks this damage, because the probe only needs a direction that separates classes, not one that captures their full feature structure.

When minority-class samples are repeatedly pushed away from a large, dense majority cluster, the gradient signal is dominated by those majority negatives, and the minority embeddings get displaced toward the sparse, underutilized regions of the hypersphere — the "poles" relative to the majority mass. Wang & Isola (2020) formalize this through the uniformity term: the loss rewards spreading all embeddings evenly, but in practice majority classes colonize broad hyperspherical caps, and minority classes are geometrically compressed into whatever angular space remains. Kang et al. (2021) in their study of decoupled contrastive learning found that representation learning and classifier learning have different sensitivities to imbalance — the encoder is less degraded than the linear head — but this obscures a real geometric cost: minority clusters tend to have smaller intra-class angular spread, meaning the encoder has collapsed within-class variation that a richer, balanced training regime would have preserved. That tight clustering looks like a virtue in nearest-neighbor retrieval (the cluster is compact and pure) but is actually suppression — features that distinguish, say, two subspecies or two disease subtypes within the minority class are gone, which is precisely what clinical or fine-grained recognition downstream tasks need. Liu et al. (2022) in BCL (Balanced Contrastive Learning) showed that rebalancing the negative sampling distribution — so minority samples appear as negatives at roughly the same rate as majority ones — shifted minority embeddings toward more central, higher-variance positions and recovered 2–4% top-1 accuracy on iNaturalist-2018, a dataset where the rarest classes have ~6× fewer samples than the most common. The practical hurt to downstream tasks is therefore two-layered: poor linear separability and collapsed intra-class structure, with standard evaluation catching only the first.

Feldman & Zhang (2020) showed in a supervised setting that memorization of tail examples comes partly at the expense of head-class generalization, and a analogous dynamic appears in contrastive learning: BCL's iNaturalist results show majority (head) classes dropping ~0.5–1% top-1 while tail classes gain 2–4%, suggesting the exchange rate heavily favors rebalancing. For practitioners, the decision should be driven by the downstream task's feature granularity requirements: if the application needs only coarse class separation (e.g., broad object categories), a mild rebalancing like BCL's square-root frequency sampling is a safe default; if the application is fine-grained (medical subtyping, species identification), you should monitor intra-class variance of embeddings directly — not just probe accuracy — across both head and tail classes during pretraining. The honest synthesis is that DAPT and adapter methods are complementary rather than competing: DAPT is appropriate when the downstream domain is broad and the pretraining mismatch is severe, while adapters are safer when the backbone serves multiple tasks and you cannot afford to shift its shared geometry — the choice should be governed by whether the deployment context is single-task or multi-task.
